note: With 654 drafts extracted, the review desk was driven against a real store for the first time -- 70 pairs, 26 of them sealed by the operator. Three tabs were found asserting something the store contradicted. Queue said every segment was 'either served ... or already decided' while 44 drafts waited on a human. Graph and Triage said 'No decisions in this store yet' underneath a badge reading 26 sealed. Ask opened on a hardcoded `en -> es` while the store's only domain was `decision -> commitment`, so the product's own answer path looked broken on a store full of answers; S.domains already carried the right value and nothing read it. All three were invisible in the source and obvious on screen.

decisions.question: What must a view show when it has nothing to show?
decisions.commitment: Why it is empty, never that the work is done. 'Nothing here' and 'nothing left to do' are different claims, and a view that conflates them asserts completion it has not checked. Each empty state now names the reason for its own emptiness and points at where the outstanding work actually is.
decisions.why: An empty state is written once, early, when the developer has no data and is imagining a finished system -- so the cheerful reading gets written down and never revisited, because the only way to catch it is to look at the tab on a store where the claim is false. The cost is asymmetric and falls on the user: a reader who sees 'nothing here' investigates, and a reader who sees 'all done' stops. Nestor's whole purpose is refusing to assert what has not been verified, and three of its own tabs were asserting completion they had never checked.

decisions.question: Graph and Triage really were empty. Why was the sentence still wrong?
decisions.commitment: Because it said 'decisions', and the rest of the page uses that word for pairs, of which the store held 70. The emptiness was true about the decision-graph tables and false in the only vocabulary the reader has. A true statement in the wrong register is read as a false one.
decisions.why: This is the failure mode that testing cannot reach, because nothing is incorrect -- the query returned zero, the template rendered it, the assertion passes. The defect lives entirely in the gap between the word the schema uses and the word the page has taught its reader, and it is only visible to somebody holding both at once. It argues for reading a UI as a reader rather than as its author, on data the author did not choose.

decisions.question: Should Ask be made to work under --read-only, since it reads like a read?
decisions.commitment: No -- reverted after reading _ask's own docstring: 'A write endpoint despite reading like a read: a passage is appended to the ledger ... An answer served without a trail is the thing Nestor exists to prevent.' The real defect was a disabled button that never said why, so it now carries the reason instead.
decisions.why: The proposal was made from the button's appearance and would have sent clicks at a server correctly refusing them. What stopped it was the docstring of the function being called -- the answer was written down at the exact place the change would have landed, and reading it took less time than the change would have. A control that refuses without explaining is a real defect, but it is a labelling defect, and the fix for it must not be to remove the refusal.

decisions.question: Most of this session's UI defects survived tests and review. What actually found them?
decisions.commitment: Looking at the page, on the operator's real data, as a reader. The markdown that rendered as source, the columns crammed to one side, the sealed rows piling up with no bottom to the list, the three lying empty states, and a regression I introduced -- inputs sized for `en` truncating `decision` -- were all invisible in a diff and immediate on screen.
decisions.why: Every one of these passed the tests, because the tests assert what the code was written to do and the defect was that the wrong thing was written. This is not an argument for fewer tests; it is the boundary of what they cover. The rule to carry forward is that a change to something a person looks at is not verified until somebody has looked at it, on data they did not invent -- and the operator's store was the ingredient that made every one of these visible at once.
